The Qibla

On this page
  • The Qibla locator
  • The 2-D compass
  • The 3-D compass

Taqwim gives the Qibla direction for your place along the shortest path on the Earth's surface, computed on the Earth's true (slightly flattened) shape. You can find it with the compass, with the Sun, on the map, or on the 2-D and 3-D compasses.

All directions in Taqwim are measured from true north. The phone's compass measures from magnetic north, so Taqwim corrects it with the magnetic declination of your place, from the World Magnetic Model.

The Qibla locator

On the home screen, tap Qibla locator. Three buttons at the top choose the way: Compass, Sun and Map.

Under the dial, a card always shows:

  • Qibla bearing: the true direction in degrees, with its compass point;
  • Magnetic bearing: the same direction measured from magnetic north, for use with an ordinary compass;
  • Magnetic declination: the angle between true and magnetic north at your place;
  • Distance to the Kaaba, in kilometres or miles (Settings → General → Distance).

Under it, Today's Qibla alignments lists the moments today when The Sun is in the Qibla direction, The Moon is in the Qibla direction, or A stick's shadow points to the Qibla. At those moments you can find the Qibla simply by facing the Sun or the Moon, or by following a shadow.

The compass method

  1. Hold the phone flat, top edge pointing ahead.
  2. Turn slowly. The large number is the direction you face; the dial turns with you, and the Qibla mark stays on the Qibla.
  3. Follow the hint, for example "Turn 27° right", until Taqwim says You are facing the Qibla.

If the direction looks wrong:

  • Move the phone in a figure-eight, away from metal, to calibrate its compass.
  • Correct the compass with the Sun, on a sunny day:
    1. Point the top edge of the phone at the Sun ("Point the top edge of the phone at the Sun, then tap").
    2. Tap Correct with the Sun. Taqwim shows the correction it applied, for example "Compass corrected with the Sun: +7°".
    3. If it also says "Large error: move away from metal and magnets", the room is disturbing the sensor. Move and try again.
    4. Remove correction cancels it. The correction lasts while the page is open and is not saved.

On iPhone and iPad, tap Enable compass if it appears, and allow access to motion and orientation.

On a device without a compass sensor, such as most computers, Taqwim says "No compass sensor: the dial is north-up. Turn yourself so that north matches a real compass." Use the bearing in degrees with a real compass, or the Sun method, or the map.

The Sun method

This method needs no sensor, only the Sun.

  1. Tap Sun. The dial now shows the Sun at the top, the Qibla mark at its angle from the Sun, and an arrow for your shadow.
  2. Follow either instruction:
    • "Face the Sun, then turn 40° left" (the number and side are for your place and time);
    • "Face along your shadow, then turn 40° right", with the Sun behind you.
  3. When the Sun or your shadow is exactly in line, Taqwim says "The Sun is in the Qibla direction now" or "Your shadow points to the Qibla now".

The Sun method cannot be used when the Sun is below the horizon, or too low or too high in the sky. Taqwim then says why, and tells you when the Sun will next be in the Qibla direction today.

The map

Tap Map to see the Qibla line drawn on a map from your place to the Kaaba. See Maps, nearby mosques and offline areas.

The 2-D compass

On the home screen, tap 2D compass. The dial turns with the phone and shows the directions of the Qibla, the Sun and the Moon. Under it, each has a row with its direction in degrees, and the Sun and Moon also their altitude above the horizon ("alt 35°"). A hollow mark means the body is below the horizon.

The large number is your heading, already corrected to true north. If it looks wrong, follow the hint at the bottom: "If the heading looks wrong, move the phone in a figure-eight away from metal."

The 3-D compass

On the home screen, tap 3D compass. It shows the sky around you as a ball: the horizon with its directions, the Qibla and its great circle, and the Sun and the Moon now with their paths for the day.

  • On a phone with a compass, the ball turns as you turn. The line under it says where the Qibla is: The Qibla is straight ahead, or for example "Qibla 32° to the right".
  • Without a sensor, drag the ball to turn it ("Drag the ball to turn it"), and tap North to bring north to the front.
